home-shifting: A household move is really three jobs stacked on top of each other: packing what you own, carrying it out of one building and into another, and putting the heavy pieces back together at the other end. Most of the cost sits in the second one. Two flats with identical contents can price very differently because one has a service lift and a loading bay and the other has four floors of stairs and a gate that closes to trucks after nine in the morning.

That is why we survey before we quote. A ten minute video walkthrough tells us how many cartons your kitchen will actually take, whether the wardrobe comes apart or has to be carried whole, which pieces need crating, and what the access looks like at both ends. From that we size the vehicle and the crew and put one number in writing. A quote given over the phone without seeing your goods is a guess, and guesses are what get revised upward on moving day.

Packing usually happens the day before the vehicle arrives, not the same morning. Crockery, glass and small electronics are wrapped and boxed first, furniture is dismantled and padded, and every carton is labelled with the room it belongs to so unloading does not turn into a search. Beds, dining tables and modular units are reassembled at the new home as part of the job. What we do not touch is civil, electrical and carpentry work: drilling new fittings, moving a geyser, or getting an air conditioner gas charged are specialist trades, and we will tell you plainly rather than attempt them.

Keep a small bag with you rather than in the truck. Documents, jewellery, medicines, chargers, house keys and anything you would not want out of sight for a day should travel with you. Everything else is listed on a shared inventory that you and the crew both sign, so if a question comes up later there is a record instead of two different memories. Transit cover is available and priced separately, and the terms are written on the quote rather than described over a call.
office-shifting: The expensive part of moving an office is not the trucks. It is the hours your team cannot work. A shift that runs into Monday morning costs far more than the quotation ever did, so office moves are planned backwards from the moment you need people logged in and working, and everything else is arranged to hit that.

In practice that means most of the work happens when the building is empty. Friday evening through Sunday is the common window, and for larger floors we split the move across two weekends so half the team is always operational. Building management usually needs notice for after hours access, a service lift booking and a list of crew names, so we start that paperwork early. A move held at the gate because nobody filed a form is an avoidable and very visible failure.

Every carton carries a label that maps to a destination: a seat number, a cabin, a store room. Workstations are photographed before dismantling so they go back the same way. Files stay in sequence rather than being tipped into boxes. On the IT side we pack and move the hardware and reinstall workstations, and we coordinate with your own IT vendor for the parts that should stay with them, which is server decommissioning, structured cabling and anything under a support contract you do not want voided.

Two things are worth deciding before we quote. First, what is actually moving: offices accumulate furniture nobody has used in years, and paying to transport it is the easiest money to save. Second, who signs off at the destination, because someone has to be there with authority to say where things go. Give us those two answers and a floor plan, and the written quote covers the whole weekend rather than the parts we could see from a phone call.
car-transport: Your car travels on a carrier, not under its own power. That is the single most important thing to understand about this service, because it explains almost everything else: why the odometer reads the same at both ends, why the tank should be nearly empty, and why the timeline depends on a truck's route rather than a driving distance.

You choose the carrier. An open carrier is the common option, cheaper and faster to schedule because more of them run on every route, with the trade off that the vehicle is exposed to weather and road dust for the journey. An enclosed carrier costs more and often waits longer for a slot, and it is the sensible choice for a new car, a premium one, or anything with paintwork you would be unhappy to see marked. Neither affects how the car is secured: wheels are locked and soft ties go over the tyres rather than the axles or suspension.

Before loading we complete a condition report. The car is photographed from every side with existing scratches, dents and stone chips recorded, and you get a copy. It takes a few minutes and it is what turns a later disagreement into a comparison of two photographs. Fuel is kept low deliberately, roughly a quarter tank or less, because a full tank adds weight and is a fire risk on a loaded carrier. Do not leave personal belongings in the cabin or boot; they are not covered and they move around in transit.

Declare aftermarket fittings when you book. Roof racks, spoilers, upgraded alloys and aftermarket audio change how the vehicle is secured and what it is worth, and an undeclared modification is the usual reason a claim gets argued. Duties, tolls and any entry tax at the destination are yours, as is RTO paperwork if you are re-registering in a new state. We move the car and hand it back with the condition report; we do not act as your agent at the transport office.
bike-transport: A motorcycle is more fragile in transit than a car, which surprises people. There is no shell around it, the weight sits high, and the parts most likely to be damaged are the ones sticking out: mirrors, levers, indicators, the exhaust and the tank. Almost all bike damage happens during loading and unloading rather than on the highway, so that is where the care goes.

The bike is wrapped before it goes anywhere. Bubble and foam over the tank and panels, stretch film over that, and padding on the levers and mirrors. For long routes or a bike worth protecting properly, we crate it in wood on request, which costs more and is the closest thing to a guarantee against handling damage. Loading is done with ramps and a crew walking it up. Nobody lifts a bike by the handlebars and nobody drops it onto a truck bed, because that is exactly how a fork gets bent.

Fuel is drained before transit. This is a safety rule rather than a preference, and it is why you should ride the tank down before pickup instead of filling up. Disconnect or remove the battery if you are storing the bike at the other end for a while. As with cars, we photograph the bike from all sides at pickup and again at delivery, and you get both sets, so the condition of the machine is a matter of record rather than argument.

Tell us about anything non standard. Crash guards, top boxes, aftermarket exhausts, raised handlebars and panniers all change the dimensions we have to plan for and the value at risk, and an undeclared accessory is the most common reason a claim runs into trouble. Registration transfer is not part of this service, and storage past the quoted period is charged separately. If you want cover, the transit insurance option is priced on the quotation rather than mentioned vaguely and forgotten.
loading-unloading: This is labour, not a move. You have already solved the vehicle, or you have a driver arriving, or a friend with a tempo, and what you actually need is a trained crew for the two hours where things get carried. That is what this service is, and pricing it separately means you are not paying for transport you do not want.

It suits a few situations well. Shifting within the same building or society, where a truck makes no sense. Receiving a consignment when there is nobody at home strong enough to bring it in. A part load where the transporter drops at the gate and the last stretch is yours to arrange. Or a move where you are handling the packing yourself and only want help with the heavy end.

The crew loads, stacks and secures. Stacking order matters more than people expect: heavy and flat at the bottom, fragile on top, nothing resting on a mattress edge, and rope or tie downs across the load so it does not shift when the vehicle brakes. At the destination the same crew unloads and places items in the right rooms. What they will not do is pack your goods, because packing is a separate service with its own materials, or reassemble furniture, which is quoted with the home shifting job.

Two things change the price and are worth mentioning when you book. Floors without a working lift, because carrying a double door refrigerator up three flights is a different job from wheeling it across a lobby. And long carry, meaning the distance between where the vehicle can legally stop and your door. Societies with a distant gate or a no entry rule for trucks can add a hundred metres each way to every single carton, and it is better to price that honestly upfront than to discover it with the crew standing on the road.
packing-unpacking: Damage is decided at the packing table, not on the road. By the time a carton is sealed, whatever is going to happen to the contents has largely been determined by how they were wrapped and what they were wrapped in. This service exists because that step is skilled work and rushing it is the most common false economy in a move.

Materials are layered rather than generic. Crockery and glassware are individually wrapped and set in cell partitions so nothing touches anything else. Electronics go back in original packaging where you still have it, and into foam and corrugation where you do not. Screens travel flat only when they are built to. Appliances are drained and secured, with the drum locked on a washing machine and the compressor kept upright on a refrigerator. Framed pictures, mirrors and glass tops are corner protected and crated when they are large enough to need it.

Every carton is labelled by room and by contents, and fragile items are photographed as they are packed. This is not paperwork for its own sake: it is what makes unpacking quick and what gives you a record if something needs to be raised later. Packing typically happens the day before loading, which spreads the work over two calmer days rather than compressing everything into one long moving morning.

Unpacking is included when you book it, and so is taking the debris away. A move generates a startling volume of cardboard, film and paper, and leaving it stacked in a new living room is a poor finish to the job. What this service does not cover is transport, loading or unloading, which are quoted separately, and storage of packed goods. If you want packing and moving as one job, home shifting is the service that bundles them and prices them together.
international-relocation: An international move runs on a different clock. Domestic shifting is measured in days, this is measured in weeks, and most of that time is spent on paperwork and vessel schedules rather than on anything physically happening to your goods. Planning backwards from the date you need to be settled, and starting early, matters more here than in any other kind of move.

The first real decision is sea or air. Sea freight is what most household goods travel on, priced by volume, and it is the sensible choice for furniture and anything you can live without for several weeks. Air freight is priced by weight, costs multiples more, and is worth it only for a small, genuinely urgent consignment: a fortnight of clothes, a laptop, documents, a child's essentials. Many families end up splitting the shipment, with a small air consignment landing first and the sea container following.

Packing to export standard is not the same as packing for a city move. Goods face humidity, handling at multiple ports and a container that may sit in the sun, so materials are heavier, moisture barriers are used, and wooden crates are built for anything fragile or high value. Timber packing has to meet treatment rules for the destination country, which is one of several requirements that are invisible until they are not met and the consignment is held.

Documentation is where shipments actually get stuck. A detailed valued inventory, your passport and visa, proof of residence and the destination country's own forms all have to agree with each other, and an inconsistency between the packing list and the declaration is the usual cause of delay. We prepare the documents with you and coordinate clearance at both ends. What remains yours are the duties and taxes the destination levies, demurrage if clearance is held up for reasons on your side, and the knowledge of what you are shipping: every country has a prohibited and restricted list covering things like alcohol, plants, seeds and certain electronics, and it is checked before packing rather than discovered at the port.
